alalal-e17439-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 4: whether one must obey authority in all things.

alalal-e17439-d1e117.summary: Turns to the second part of Lombard's text, beginning 'Hic oritur quaestio non transilienda silentio'.

alalal-e17439-d1e129.summary: States the first of two questions on this part: whether one must obey authority in all things.

alalal-e17439-d1e139.summary: States the second question: whether one must resist the power of the devil.

alalal-e17439-d1e146.summary: First objection from Bernard's De praecepto et dispensatione: a prelate may demand nothing beyond what I vowed, so one need not obey a prelate in all things.

alalal-e17439-d1e165.summary: Second objection from Bernard: a subject is neither to be held back short of the vow nor compelled beyond the law of observance.

alalal-e17439-d1e179.summary: Contrary authority from Bernard: perfect obedience knows no law and is not confined by limits, so it obeys in all.

alalal-e17439-d1e193.summary: Hugh of Saint Victor: obedience is the virtue that embraces all commands as to be fulfilled, unless the authority of the one commanding stands in the way.

alalal-e17439-d1e207.summary: Ecclesiasticus 4:32: do not resist the face of the powerful; so one should resist in nothing.

alalal-e17439-d1e217.summary: Colossians 3:20 commands children to obey parents in all things, all the more spiritual parents, so authority must be obeyed in all things.

alalal-e17439-d1e228.summary: Jerome to Rusticus: believe whatever the superior commands to be salutary, and do not judge the superior's sentence; the subject's duty is to obey and fulfil commands.

alalal-e17439-d1e251.summary: Gregory: consider not the extent of the command but the dignity of the one commanding.

alalal-e17439-d1e263.summary: The Gospel: 'he who hears you hears me'; God must be heard in all things, so the prelate too.

alalal-e17439-d1e274.summary: Benedict's Rule: if a prelate commands the impossible, one must try; all the more must one obey in all possible things.

alalal-e17439-d1e288.summary: Solution, following Bernard: perfect obedience, belonging to charity and liberty, knows no limit, while obedience of justice is bounded by the vow and can be extended only by charity. Following the masters, one must also distinguish full from limited power. Full power is to be obeyed in all that belongs to power, but not in commands to sin, which belong to impotence rather than power, since power is given for building up, not destroying. Within that, perfect obedience obeys in all goods, while obedience of justice obeys only where bound by vow or office, as with the scribes on Moses' seat. Under limited power one is bound in justice only as a subject, by a superior's command or vow, but may obey further out of charity, never against vow or a superior's command.
claims: Commands to sin are not to be obeyed, since they belong to impotence rather than authority.
Obedience of justice is limited by vow and office, while perfect obedience out of charity extends to all good things.
Obedience to a limited authority may never contravene a vow or the command of a higher superior.
concepts: perfect obedience vs obedience of justice

alalal-e17439-d1e378.summary: This resolves all: the first authorities concern obedience owed in justice, the second the perfection of charity in obeying.

alalal-e17439.summary: Article 4 asks whether authority must be obeyed in all things. Bernard limits a prelate's demands to what was vowed, while other authorities (Bernard on perfect obedience, Hugh, Scripture, Jerome, Gregory, Benedict) urge obedience in all. Albert reconciles them through two distinctions. Obedience of justice is bounded by vow and office, while perfect obedience, rooted in charity and liberty, extends to every good. Full authority is obeyed in all that belongs to it, but never in commands to sin, which express impotence rather than power, since power is given for building up. Under limited authority one is bound only as a subject and may go further out of charity, but never against a vow or a higher superior.
claims: No authority is to be obeyed in commanding sin.
Obedience owed in justice is limited by vow and office, while perfect obedience from charity extends to all goods.
Authority is given for building up, so sinful commands fall outside it.
concepts: perfect obedience vs obedience of justice
